We recruited a total of 36 young men into the study.
The study received full Office of Research Ethics Committee, Northern Ireland, approval.

The study population was drawn exclusively from Northern Ireland, a region that has witnessed a dramatic increase in suicide among young men in the past 10 to 15 years (Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency, 2010a).
Support was received in the form of a grant from the Northern Ireland, Department of Health, Social Services and Public Safety (DHSSPS, NI), Public Health Agency, Research and Development Office.

A core criterion for involvement was that participants had been actively suicidal at some time in their lives, ascertained through use of the Beck Scale for Suicidal Ideation–Worst. This is a well-validated tool for assessing suicidal intent at its worst, irrespective of time elapsed (Beck, Brown, & Steer, 1997; Beck, Brown, Steer, Dahlsgaard, & Grisham, 1999). All participants scored as having significant suicidal ideation, with 85% scoring as having severe to profound suicidal ideation.

The need to allow participants the opportunity to express in personally meaningful ways the circumstances of their suicidal behavior prompted our use of in-depth interviews as the means of data collection. All interviews were audio-recorded, with permission.

evidence.section_title: Implications of Findings  for Service Delivery
evidence.quote: Our research, undertaken specifically with young men who have experienced suicidal behavior and/or thinking

[/page/0/Text/6] Our analysis yielded three core categories: widening access and bolstering proactive outreach, on becoming a man, and equipping young men for future challenges. Collectively, these categories suggest key features and processes of appropriate service configuration and clinical care: (a) services that reach out proactively serve to encourage young men's initial and ongoing engagement; (b) care delivered over the long term ensures a necessary focus on a meaningful future life; (c) mental health professionals (MHPs) are centrally involved alongside significant others, including those with personal experience of suicide; and (d) the development of a vital interpersonal connection is based on MHPs actively communicating their empathy, open-mindedness, and interest in a young man's unique biography.

International research consistently demonstrates reluctance on the part of young men to engage with health services, including in relation to mental health distress (Biddle, Gunnell, Sharp, & Donovan, 2004; Burke & McKeon, 2007; Centre for Suicide Prevention, 2007). Young men have been shown to be vulnerable to seeing mental distress and concomitant help seeking in negative terms (Barney, Griffiths, Jorm, & Christensen, 2006; Cleary, 2005; Stanistreet, Gabbay, Jeffrey, & Taylor, 2004). Consequently, they not only are less likely to disclose their own emotional distress but also are inhibited from accessing professional and/or lay support (Rickwood, Deane, & Wilson, 2007). These negative perceptions have been understood in three principal, overlapping ways. The first way is as a result of a cultural stigmatizing of mental illness (Burke & McKeon, 2007; Corrigan, 2005), on the basis of which those labeled as mentally ill are demeaned and marginalized. Responding to such cultural cues, young men are prompted to hide their own emotional distress as a means of avoiding deeply negative stereotyping and concomitant treatment by others. The second way is in terms of gender socialization, encompassing a number of related social processes that together work to uphold the 'male' attributes of emotional robustness and independence. Consequently, young men view help seeking for mental distress as implying weakness and vulnerability and, therefore, as something to be avoided (Gulliver, Griffiths, & Christensen, 2010). Finally, (young) men have been ascribed a relative lack of emotional competence and consequent poor recognition of personal mental distress, further inhibiting disclosure and help seeking (Möller-Leinkühler, 2002; Rickwood, Deane, Wilson, & Ciarrochi, 2005).

evidence.section_title: Widening Access and Bolstering  Proactive Outreach
evidence.quote: Risk: Participants' descriptions of their (non)engagement with services suggested that the current organization and delivery of formal mental health care could discourage young men from access (see Figure 1). They highlighted the need for greater outreach and better advertizing, mentioning difficulties they had experienced in learning about existing services, frequently doing so only after their suicide attempt(s). Referral mechanisms and processes were perceived to further hinder access. There was a sense that if a young man did not satisfy certain predetermined criteria, he could not be referred and thus could not access services: ... Participants were acutely aware of the stigma associated with using suicide-related services. Consequently, they articulated the need for service(s) that were discrete, informal, and manifestly not associated (at least exclusively) with mental (ill) health. ... Furthermore, the young men's pervasive sense of disconnection from humanity (that "nobody cares") diminished on encountering manifestly supportive MHPs. Recovery: They highlighted the need for greater outreach and better advertizing, mentioning difficulties they had experienced in learning about existing services, frequently doing so only after their suicide attempt(s). ... For participants, these perceived barriers underscored the potential of a variety of forms of proactive outreach. Examples included educational school-based programs, enhanced media advertising (e.g., radio and television), and programs delivered in a variety of settings (e.g., youth clubs, colleges of further education). Providing outreach through mobile phone text messaging and Webbased social networking was also seen as appropriate, reflecting current patterns of interaction and communication among young people generally: ... The provision of drop-in, community-based centers, capable of affording social interaction (e.g., sports-based activities) and a generally laid-back environment, received widespread support: ... In terms of clinical care, participants emphasized the value of engaging with mental health professionals (MHPs) who were explicitly supportive. A firm interpersonal connection was achieved as a result of the MHPs not only possessing but actively communicating relevant attitudes and behaviors. These appeared to be the principal interventions that the MHPs made use of, whereby they were perceived to be present, holistically, with the young men. In this context, participants highlighted the importance of a sense of mutual respect, typically manifested by seeing themselves as being treated as an adult individual, not being talked down to: ... The development of this relationship involved additional processes that worked to establish trust. These included active listening and responding in manifestly nonjudgmental ways on the part of MHPs. ... The resultant sense of no longer being alone had a distinct countering effect on the young men's suicidal perspectives: ... The therapeutic value of such a perspective was made clear as participants described the feelings that were stimulated as a result of "their" MHP demonstrating concern. They were aware that they needed to feel that they mattered; they needed to feel that someone cared about them: ... Well, that's what helped me, knowing I had someone who actually cared.

[page/4/Text/10] Participants referenced a range of perceptions that contributed to their low self-esteem, levels of personal stress, and, ultimately, their increased risk for suicide (see Figure 2). The first perception was their understandings of what it was to be a successful man, which involved, among others, the following limiting constructs: that successful or "real" men have high-powered (meaningful) jobs, lots of money, access to girls, are certainly not gay, are emotionally tough, do not need help, do not admit intrapersonal difficulties, and certainly do not admit to psychological problems: [page/6/Text/3] Participants referred to a wide variety of problems, each of which, to a greater or lesser extent, elevated their risk of suicide. Such problems included physically, emotionally, and sexually dysfunctional or abusive childhoods and family backgrounds; poor or low self-image; relationship difficulties and breakdowns; drug abuse and addiction; and general and specific anxieties. [page/5/Text/9] Participants stressed the therapeutic value of being able to mix with people who had survived similar circumstances; this helped them to appreciate they were "not the only ones like this." Moreover, they were able to verbalize how they were feeling in a forum in which they were not afraid of being labeled as crazy or weird. Such contact and interaction served to normalize suicide, normalize their difficulties and, ultimately, normalize them as human beings: [page/6/Text/1] Finally, hearing these testimonies served as a protective factor against future suicide attempts. [page/6/Text/3] In some cases, the young men had been able to access counseling therapy (e.g., cognitive behavioral therapy [CBT]) within mental health services. These young men had invariably found such therapy to be of benefit:

evidence.section_title: Equipping Young Men  for Future Challenges
evidence.quote: This category is concerned with the processes and activities with which the young men engaged on their journey toward recovery from suicidality (see Figure 3). Participants repeatedly talked about their endeavors to find new meaning after their suicide attempt(s). These efforts were bound up with a sense of starting anew, deliberately restructuring their lives. There was a distinct process of leaving "what has gone" in the past, to some extent reframing how some of this past was viewed, and seeking a new perspective on their present and future. Identifying new meaning appeared, in some cases, to be prefaced with a growing sense of discontent and dissatisfaction with their lives: It just seemed like a lifetime of failure, like no sort of, you know, jumping from job to job. . . . I also, ehm, have a son from another relationship that I've never seen as well. It just seems, looking back on my adult life, it just stemmed from like one failure to another. And then the gambling on top of that, and it just, it just sort of seemed that everything, that my life was a complete failure. New meaning was variously conceived and pursued depending on a young man's individual circumstances and outlook. These included forming new, or renewing former, significant relationships; (re)developing family bonds; career and employment progression; personal development (e.g., voluntary work, acquiring new skills, returning to education); exploring spirituality-related issues; and helping others experiencing similar problems with suicide: So I took a positive approach to everything. I chose to do that, and that was the thing for me, like empowering. I chose to stop allowing it to happen to me. . . . And for me now, I have . . . worked with our own GPs [general practitioners] to promote mental health awareness, and to have different numbers for different groups.7 Frequently, finding (new) meaning in life was the direct opposite of the events and experiences that contributed to participants' increased suicidality in the first place. For example, although dysfunctional family dynamics was reported to be a significant contributor to suicidal ideation, having loving and supportive relationships with family members was described as bringing new meaning to their lives: "Now things have got very, very good. I have lovely children, and I have three boys, and I really enjoy my life now and I realize what I do have." The young men were also acutely aware of the powerful protective role that having close, concerned family members could play in relation to their risk of suicide. The (re)establishment of family bonds facilitated the development of a profound sense of guilt concerning the detrimental impact of their suicidal behavior on others and a consequent unwillingness to hurt their family (through the action of harming themselves): "But it's a dreadfully selfish thing, and I just . . . I couldn't deal with, handle the thought of how much pain I was going to be causing, well, my family and my friends." Finally, this category captures the importance of a developing appreciation among young men that recovery from their suicidality was, inevitably, a long-term process and that within this extended time frame, a degree of hard work was required: It took a while for us to make headway . . . but I guess I stuck with it and he [counselor] stuck with it, so we did make progress eventually, you know. At the start it didn't seem as if we were getting anywhere. This appreciation is integrally bound up with participants beginning to pick up the threads of their life and, in essence, learning to live again. For some, this process included making sense of their suicidality. None referred to this sense making in the past tense or as something they had completed. This shifted the sense of existential crisis from "What do I have to live for?" to "How do I go on living in the context of surviving a suicide attempt?" In addition, it was evident that a number of inter- and intrapersonal processes were involved, not least the continued support from MHPs and fellow travelers on the path to recovery: Every now and again the thought would still sorta creep in, but I've basically just, my plan has been trying to teach myself as not to have it as an option . . . So that's more or less worked, but like as I say, it just now and again sorta creeps in but I just keep . . . sorta tell myself that that can't be a choice, that's not an option. The regularity with which participants spoke of the need to make sense of their suicidality in the context of moving forward with their lives highlights the importance of these processes, particularly as they helped strengthen their connections with humanity.
